nameStory: The forget-me-not gets its romantic name from European folklore, where a knight picking these flowers for his beloved fell into a river and threw the bouquet to her, calling out "forget me not" as he drowned. The "water" part of this species' name comes from its love of wet places, distinguishing it from its drier-ground cousins.
description: Water forget-me-not is a delicate perennial wildflower that forms low, spreading patches along streams, pond edges, and other wet areas. It grows 6-24 inches tall with soft, fuzzy stems that often sprawl along the ground before turning upward. The plant is crowned with clusters of tiny, sky-blue flowers that have bright yellow centers, creating carpet-like displays in early summer. Each individual flower is only about 1/4 inch across, but they bloom in such profusion that they can blanket entire wetland areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny sky-blue flowers (occasionally pink or white) with five rounded petals and bright yellow centers, arranged in curved, scorpion-tail-like clusters that unfurl as they bloom

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oblong, soft leaves that feel slightly fuzzy or hairy to the touch, with no teeth along the edges and a prominent central vein

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing perennial that spreads by creeping stems (stolons), often forming dense mats in wet areas with stems that root where they touch the ground

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Soft, hollow stems covered in fine hairs that give them a slightly rough, fuzzy texture when you run your fingers along them

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny, smooth, shiny brown nutlets that develop in groups of four at the base of each flower cluster

habitat: Water forget-me-not thrives in consistently moist to wet soils along stream banks, pond edges, marshes, wet meadows, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It prefers partial shade but tolerates full sun if the soil stays wet, and often grows alongside other moisture-loving plants like watercress, wild mint, and various sedges. You'll find it from sea level up to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy rosettes of leaves, with flower buds beginning to form in late spring as distinctive curved, coiled clusters.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period from late May through August, with masses of tiny blue flowers creating spectacular displays along waterways and in wet meadows.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse, while the plant may continue blooming sporadically until frost; leaves begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, but the creeping root system survives underground, ready to send up new shoots in spring.

funFact: The flower clusters grow in a distinctive coiled shape that botanists call 'scorpioid' because it resembles a scorpion's curled tail - the flowers actually open from the inside of the curl outward, which is why you'll often see buds and open flowers on the same spiral-shaped cluster.
confusionNotes: Water forget-me-not can be confused with other forget-me-not species, but it's the only one that truly loves wet feet - if you find forget-me-nots growing right at the water's edge or in consistently soggy soil, it's likely this species. Memory trick: 'water forget-me-not needs water, forgot-me-nots in dry spots are not.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'true forget-me-not' in some references, water forget-me-not is actually native to Europe and Asia, not New England. It has naturalized so successfully in our wetlands that many people assume it's native, but it's technically an introduced species that arrived with European settlers.
compareHints: Water forget-me-not is distinguished from other forget-me-not species by its preference for wet habitats and its perennial, mat-forming growth habit. Field forget-me-not and early forget-me-not are annuals that prefer drier soils, while wood forget-me-not grows in moist but well-drained woodland soils rather than truly wet areas. The water species also tends to have larger, more vibrant blue flowers than most of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Blue forget-me-not is the most rigid and unbranched of all New England forget-me-nots, with distinctly smaller flowers than its relatives.
Wood forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring drier woodland soils versus wet areas, and it has a more compact growth habit.
Field forget-me-not differs from water forget-me-not by preferring dry, disturbed soil rather than wet areas, and having more pronounced patent hairs on its stems.
Unlike the common water forget-me-not which stays bright blue and grows in wet areas, changing forget-me-not prefers drier disturbed soil and shows its telltale color progression.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, bay forget-me-not stands out for having the smallest flowers and most relaxed growth habit.
Among New England's forget-me-nots, early forget-me-not is the smallest and most easily overlooked.
